Alessandro Volta is a physicist. Throughout his life, Volta enjoyed a certain amount of closeness with the emperor who conferred upon him numerous honours.
Which one below is best known as a chemist?
Wallace Carothers is a chemist. Carothers was a group leader at the DuPont Experimental Station laboratory, near Wilmington, Delaware, where most polymer research was done.
What is the atomic number of Carbon?
Carbon (from Latin carbo 'coal') is a chemical element; it has symbol C and atomic number 6.
In what year was Bernard Arnault born?
Bernard Arnault: Bernard Jean Étienne Arnault (born 5 March 1949) is a French businessman.
In what year was Radon discovered?
Radon is a chemical element; it has symbol Rn and atomic number 86.
In what year was Adenosine triphosphate discovered?
Adenosine triphosphate: When consumed in a metabolic process, ATP converts either to adenosine diphosphate (ADP) or to adenosine monophosphate (AMP).
Mil Mi-26: Mil Moscow Helicopter Plant. The Mil Mi-26 (Russian: Миль Ми-26, NATO reporting name: Halo) is a Soviet/Russian heavy transport helicopter.
Which country is Focke-Wulf Fw 190 from?
Focke-Wulf Fw 190: Germany. Along with its well-known counterpart, the Messerschmitt Bf 109, the Fw 190 became the backbone of the Jagdwaffe (Fighter Force) of the Luftwaffe.
Who is credited with discovering Tantalum?
Tantalum: Anders Gustaf Ekeberg. Tantalum is a chemical element; it has symbol Ta and atomic number 73.
Who is credited with discovering L'Hôpital's rule?
L'Hôpital's rule: Johann Bernoulli. The differentiation of the numerator and denominator often simplifies the quotient or converts it to a limit that can be directly evaluated by continuity.
Who is credited with discovering Sulfur?
Sulfur: Antoine Lavoisier. Sulfur (American spelling or sulphur (Commonwealth spelling) is a chemical element; it has symbol S and atomic number 16.
A key figure of the Scottish Enlightenment, this thinker is often called the "father of economics" and is best known for "The Theory of Moral Sentiments" and "The Wealth of Nations" — who is it?
Adam Smith was Scottish economist and philosopher (1723–1790).
The simplest pnictogen hydride, with the formula NH3, this pungent gas is also a common nitrogenous waste in living things — what is it?
Ammonia is an inorganic chemical compound of nitrogen and hydrogen with the formula NH3.
Linked to smoking, high blood pressure and older age, this silent widening of the body's main artery to over 1.5 times normal size can suddenly rupture with severe abdominal pain — what condition?
Aortic aneurysm is an enlargement (dilatation) of the aorta to greater than 1.5 times normal size.
This gram-positive, spore-forming bacterium was the first ever proven experimentally to cause disease, laying the groundwork for germ theory in 1876 — which microbe?
Bacillus anthracis is a gram-positive and rod-shaped bacterium that causes anthrax, a deadly disease to livestock and, occasionally, to humans.
Present in every living cell and abundant in liver and meats, this B vitamin acts as an enzyme cofactor and takes its name from the Greek for 'life' — what is it?
Biotin (also known as vitamin B7 and vitamin H) is one of the B vitamins - a group of essential dietary micronutrients.
This outdated 19th-century term for what's now called acute or chronic nephritis was marked by swelling and albumin showing up in the urine — what was it called?
Bright's disease is a historical classification of kidney diseases that are described in modern medicine as acute or chronic nephritis.
Chili peppers likely make this hydrophobic compound to deter hungry mammals and fungi — yet it's exactly what gives them their burning, pungent heat. What is it?
Capsaicin (8-methyl-N-vanillyl-6-nonenamide) (commonly) is a toxin that is the main active component of chili peppers and gives them their distinct pungent, "spicy" or "hot" taste.
This woody perennial herb with bright blue flowers is cultivated for salad greens and a root that's roasted and ground as a coffee substitute. What plant is it?
Chicory (Cichorium intybus) is a somewhat woody, perennial herbaceous plant of the family Asteraceae, usually with bright blue flowers, rarely white or pink.

Native to tropical Africa and Asia, this genus of flowering shrubs and small trees in the Rubiaceae family produces caffeine-rich seeds that are roasted and ground into a beloved beverage worldwide — which genus?
Coffea is a genus of flowering plants in the family Rubiaceae. The seeds of some species, called coffee beans, are roasted and ground to brew into various coffee beverages.
These echinoderms come in stalked "sea lily" and free-swimming "feather star" forms, with mouths on their upper surface ringed by feeding arms — what class of marine animal is it?
Crinoid are marine invertebrates that make up the class Crinoidea.
Its genus name translates to 'two-crested lizard,' honoring the twin head-crests found on fossils unearthed in Arizona in the 1940s — which Early Jurassic predator is this?
Dilophosaurus (dy-, -foh-) is a genus of theropod dinosaurs that lived in what is now North America during the Early Jurassic, about 186 million years ago.
Despite common belief, this shocking South American fish belongs to the knifefish order and is more closely related to catfish than its name implies — what is it?
Electric eel are a genus, Electrophorus, of neotropical freshwater fish from South America in the family Gymnotidae, of which they are the only members of the subfamily Electrophorinae.
This U.S. Marine turned professor wrote a 1981 memoir of his WWII combat, later adapted into a Ken Burns documentary and an HBO miniseries where he was played by Joseph Mazzello — who was he?
Eugene Sledge (November 4, 1923 - March 3, 2001) was a United States Marine, university professor, and author.

This region of the upper limb, running between the elbow and the wrist, contains two long bones, the radius and the ulna, and is technically distinct from the 'arm' proper in anatomy — what is it called?
Forearm is the region of the upper limb between the elbow and the wrist. It is homologous to the region of the leg that lies between the knee and the ankle joints, the crus.

This heavy, slow-moving reptile native to the southwestern US and northwestern Mexico is the only venomous lizard found in the United States, though its sluggish nature makes it rarely dangerous — what animal is it?
Gila monster (Heloderma suspectum) is a species of venomous lizard native to the Southwestern United States and the northwestern Mexican state of Sonora.
This perception occurs with no external stimulus at all, yet feels completely real to the person experiencing it — distinct from dreaming, illusions, or ordinary imagination — name this phenomenon?
Hallucination is a perception in the absence of an external context stimulus that has the compelling sense of reality.
The largest of the eusocial wasps, some species in this genus can exceed 50 millimetres in length. What insect is it?
Hornet are wasps of the genus Vespa in the subfamily Vespinae (the vespine wasps).
Representing about three-quarters of circulating antibodies in humans, which type of antibody is released by plasma B cells?
Immunoglobulin G (IgG) is a type of antibody.
Enlisting as a valet named 'Jean' on Bougainville's expedition, this expert botanist disguised herself as a man and became the first woman to sail all the way around the globe — who was she?

Jeanne Baret (27 July 1740 - 5 August 1807) was a French explorer, naturalist, and botanist who is recognised as the first woman to have completed a voyage of circumnavigation of the globe, which she did via boat.
The world's longest venomous snake with an average length of 3.18 to 4 meters, endemic to Asia and widely distributed though not commonly encountered. What is it?
King cobra (Ophiophagus hannah) is a species complex of snakes endemic to Asia.
Used to treat an underactive thyroid and even a severe form called myxedema coma, this synthetic version of thyroxine (T4) takes about six weeks to reach a steady blood level — what's this drug?
Levothyroxine is a synthetic form of the thyroid hormone thyroxine (T4). It is used to treat thyroid hormone deficiency (hypothyroidism), including a severe form known as myxedema coma.
Enclosed in a fibrous capsule and linked throughout the body by lymphatic vessels, these kidney-shaped organs filter foreign particles and house the immune system's B and T cells — what are they?
Lymph node is a kidney-shaped organ of the lymphatic system and the adaptive immune system.

This English silversmith-turned-industrialist partnered with James Watt to install hundreds of steam engines, then modernized the Royal Mint and struck millions of coins for Britain and beyond — who was he?
Matthew Boulton (3 September 1728 - 17 August 1809) was an English businessman, inventor, mechanical engineer, and silversmith.

This large-scale industrial activity extracts everything from coal and gemstones to rock salt and potash from the Earth, providing raw materials that can't be grown or feasibly manufactured — what is this activity called?
Mining is the extraction of geological materials and minerals from Earth's surface.

This European twin-engine military helicopter was the first production helicopter ever built with entirely fly-by-wire flight controls, coming in both troop-transport and naval anti-submarine variants — what aircraft is it?
NHIndustries NH90 is a medium-sized European twin-engine multi-role military helicopter.
What organic molecule, composed of a nitrogenous base, a five-carbon sugar, and a phosphate group, serves as the basic building block of both DNA and RNA?
Nucleotide are organic molecules composed of a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and a phosphate.
This rare silvery-white metal, discovered in 1802 and named after a newly found asteroid, is part of the six-element platinum group and has the lowest melting point among them. What element is it?
Palladium is a chemical element; it has the symbol Pd and atomic number 46.
Fill in the blank: “____ (born 12 January 1971) is a Danish convicted murderer and former entrepreneur.”

Peter Madsen (born 12 January 1971) is a Danish convicted murderer and former entrepreneur. Peter Langkjær Madsen (Danish: [ˈpʰe̝ˀtɐ ˈlɑŋˌkʰeˀɐ̯ ˈmæsn̩]; born 12 January 1971) is a Danish convicted murderer and former entrepreneur.
Reaching 30 to 50 meters tall and mostly found near rivers and wetlands, this tree genus's hybrid form has proven so tolerant of urban pollution it lines the streets of London — what's the genus?
Platanus is a genus consisting of a small number of tree species.
A single long chain of amino acids is called a polypeptide — string enough of them together and you get this folded macromolecule whose 3D shape determines what job it does. What is it?
Protein are large biomolecules and macromolecules that comprise one or more long chains of amino acid residues.
A canine native to the southeastern United States, intermediate in size between the coyote and gray wolf. For a century its taxonomic classification has been contentious. What is it?
Red wolf (Canis rufus) is a canine native to the southeastern United States.
Mostly used in wear-resistant electrical contacts and thick-film resistors, which rare, chemically unreactive platinum-group metal has atomic number 44?
Ruthenium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ru and atomic number 44.
This veteran of six spaceflights was the first Russian cosmonaut to fly aboard NASA's Space Shuttle, on mission STS-60 — who is he?
Sergei Krikalev (born 27 August 1958) is a Russian mechanical engineer and former cosmonaut.
Made simply from ice mixed with fruit juice or purée, plus the occasional splash of wine or honey, this dairy-free frozen treat goes by what name?
Sorbet is a frozen dessert made using ice combined with fruit juice, fruit pure, or other ingredients, such as wine, liqueur, or honey.
First flown in 1967 with its crew sitting side by side under variable-sweep wings, this Soviet bomber earned the NATO codename 'Fencer' — what is it?
Sukhoi Su-24 (NATO reporting name: Fencer) is a supersonic, all-weather tactical bomber developed in the Soviet Union.
What academic discipline studies religious belief from within a faith perspective, focusing on the nature of divinity, revelation, and the history behind organized religion?
Theology is the study of religious belief from a religious perspective, with a focus on the nature of divinity and the history behind religion.

Picture a spider that never learned to spin: these extinct arachnids lacked silk-producing spinnerets and wore an abdomen split into three or five distinct plates. Which order, known from the Silurian to the Permian?
Trigonotarbida is a group of extinct arachnids whose fossil record extends from the late Silurian to the early Permian (Pridoli to Sakmarian).

First described by John Edward Gray in 1821, this family of small feliform mammals spans Africa, southern Europe, and Asia on both sides of the Wallace Line, and includes the genets — name the family?
Viverridae is a family of small to medium-sized feliform mammals, comprising 14 genera with 33 species.
Twice Egypt's Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, this archaeologist has dug across the Nile Delta, the Western Desert, and the Upper Nile Valley — who is he?
Zahi Hawass (born May 28, 1947) is an Egyptian archaeologist, Egyptologist, and former Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, a position he held twice.
Native to Africa and Yemen, this drought-resistant tree species has individuals radiocarbon-dated to over 1,275 years old — what is it?
Adansonia digitata: Species of plant native to Africa.
Brother of a concert pianist and son of an astronomer, this Russian mathematician built the foundational theory of stability in dynamical systems — who was he?
Formed naturally around volcanic vents and on burning coal dumps, this white crystalline salt is mildly acidic in solution and is used as both a fertilizer and food additive — which compound?
Ammonium chloride: Chemical compound. Ammonium chloride is an inorganic chemical compound with the chemical formula NH4Cl, also written as [NH4]Cl.

Native to the Americas from northern Mexico to northern Argentina, this flowering plant genus is the largest in the arum family and includes types nicknamed flamingo flower and pigtail plant. What genus is it?
Anthurium: Genus of plants. Anthurium (Schott, 1829) is a genus of about 1,000 species of flowering plants, the largest genus of the arum family, Araceae.
These chitin-armored invertebrates must shed their exoskeletons to grow and circulate haemolymph through an open body cavity — and may number up to ten million species. What are they?
Arthropod: Phylum of invertebrates with jointed exoskeletons.

Flown by the Royal Air Force's Red Arrows display team, this British jet-powered advanced trainer has been license-built in India by Hindustan Aeronautics, with over 1,000 sold to 18 countries — which aircraft?
BAE Systems Hawk: Military training aircraft family.

With his former teacher Alfred North Whitehead, this English philosopher co-wrote Principia Mathematica and, alongside G. E. Moore, led the British 'revolt against idealism.' Who was this founder of analytic philosophy?
Bertrand Russell: English mathematician and philosopher (1872–1970)
Conceived for Pan Am as a jet two-and-a-half times the size of the 707, this wide-body, led by designer Joe Sutter, rolled out of the world's largest building in 1968 — which airliner is it?
Boeing 747: American wide-body four-engined jet long-range aircraft.

Branching from the windpipe at a landmark called the carina, these airway passages narrow progressively through several orders before losing cartilage support and changing name entirely — what are they called?
Bronchus: Airway in the respiratory tract.
Bearing distinctive fatty humps and used for milk, meat, and transport across deserts for millennia, which ungulate comes in a common one-humped form and a rarer two-humped form?
Its raw shell and seed are actually toxic until roasted or steamed, and the tropical American tree it grows on also yields a fleshy 'apple' — what is this familiar snack?
Cashew: Flowering plant in the family Anacardiaceae.
Beyond the resistance-measuring "bridge" that carries his name, this English inventor also gave us the stereoscope, the English concertina, and the Playfair cipher — who was he?
Charles Wheatstone: English physicist and inventor (1802–1875)

Unlike oysters and mussels, which attach to a surface, or scallops, which live near the bottom, this bivalve mollusk instead burrows into sand or mud on the sea floor — what is it, the namesake of a popular chowder?
Clam: Common name for several kinds of bivalve mollusc.

A summer migrant to Europe and Asia that winters in Africa, this bird tricks other species into raising its young by laying eggs that mimic the host's, and even disguises itself as a hawk — what bird is it?
Common cuckoo: Species of bird. It is a brood parasite, which means it lays eggs in the nests of other bird species, particularly of dunnocks, meadow pipits, and reed warblers.
Nicknamed the mosquito hawk, which long-legged insect of the superfamily Tipuloidea is often mistaken for an oversized mosquito?
Crane fly: Superfamily of flies. The larvae of crane flies are known commonly as leatherjackets.
This World Wide Web content sits on overlay networks that use the Internet but cannot be reached with an ordinary browser. What does reaching it require?
The dark web is World Wide Web content that exists on darknets — overlay networks that use the Internet but require specific software, configurations or authorization to access.
Produced by the enzyme 5α-reductase acting on a more familiar male sex hormone, this compound is a more potent driver of prostate growth, sebum, and body hair — which hormone?
Sometimes called 'word blindness,' this learning disability makes it hard to spell, sound out words, and read quickly, and often co-occurs with ADHD — what is it?
The tallest and heaviest of all living penguins, this flightless Antarctic bird can top 45 kilograms and sports bright-yellow ear patches — which species is it?
Emperor penguin: Large flightless seabird endemic to Antarctica.
This Marine-turned-professor's 1981 memoir about fighting at Peleliu and Okinawa later inspired Ken Burns's The War and HBO's The Pacific, where he was played by Joseph Mazzello — who is he?
Made up mostly of undigested food broken down by gut bacteria, this bodily waste is expelled through the anus and can even be dried for fuel or used as fertilizer — what is it?
Feces: Solid or semisolid remains of undigested food.

First described by 19th-century French psychiatrists Charles Lasègue and Jules Falret, this rare condition — also called shared psychotic disorder — lets one person's delusion spread to another. What is it called?

Folie à deux: Shared psychosis, a psychotic disorder. The disorder, first conceptualized in 19th century French psychiatry by Charles Lasègue and Jules Falret, is also known as Lasègue–Falret syndrome.

Named after Scottish naturalist Alexander Garden and first proposed in 1753 by botanist Jane Colden, this fragrant flowering genus in the coffee family is native to Africa, Asia and Australia — which plant genus?
Gardenia: Genus of flowering plants in the coffee family Rubiaceae.
Nicknamed the blue dragon, this pelagic sea slug floats upside down using surface tension and a stomach gas bubble, and feeds on the Portuguese man o' war — what is it?
With long, whip-like antennae and a global range except Antarctica, this insect family — known as true crickets — includes burrowing giants that dig meter-deep tunnels. What is the family called?
Gryllidae: Family of crickets. The family Gryllidae contains the subfamilies and genera which entomologists now term true crickets.
Native to North America, this genus of roughly 50 flowering plant species is better known by its common name — the sunflowers — and includes food crops for humans and livestock alike — which genus?

Helianthus: Genus of flowering plants, the sunflowers. Helianthus is a genus comprising around 50 species of annual and perennial flowering plants in the daisy family Asteraceae commonly known as sunflowers.
This extinct archaic human was the first to evolve a humanlike body and gait, the first to leave Africa for Asia and Europe, and the first to wield fire — who were they?
Homo erectus: Extinct species of archaic human. Homo erectus ( lit. 'upright man') is an extinct species of archaic human from the Pleistocene, spanning nearly 2 million years.
Distinct from a process that adds more cells, this one is an increase in the size of individual cells, like the uterus enlarging during pregnancy — what's it called?
Hypertrophy: Increase in the size of biological cells. Hypertrophy can lead to a relative increase in the volume of a tissue or organ, and contributes to the overall growth of an organism.
The global network of networks links private, public, academic, business and government networks using which protocol suite?
The Internet is the global system of interconnected computer networks that uses the Internet protocol suite (TCP/IP) to communicate between networks and devices.
This Swiss psychologist's theory of cognitive development in children gave rise to a field he called genetic epistemology — who was he?
The fifth planet from the Sun is a gas giant whose mass exceeds that of every other planet in the Solar System put together — by roughly what factor?

Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun and the largest in the Solar System, a gas giant with a mass nearly 2.5 times that of all the other planets combined and slightly less than one-thousandth the mass of the Sun.

Until a 2020 taxonomic overhaul split many of its 261 species into 25 new genera, this rod-shaped, gram-positive bacterial genus formed a major part of the human gut and vaginal microbiota — what genus?
Lactobacillus: Genus of bacteria. Lactobacillus forms biofilms in the vaginal and gut microbiota, allowing them to persist in harsh environmental conditions and maintain ample populations.
This fibrous connective tissue links bone to bone in every one of the 30,000 known amniote species, and in birds it even anchors flight feathers to bone — what is it?

With nearly 5,000 species, these wingless parasitic insects spend their whole lives on a single warm-blooded host, either chewing skin and feathers or piercing the skin to feed on blood — what are they?
Louse: Infraorder of insects. Louse (pl.: lice) is the common name for any member of the infraorder Phthiraptera, which contains nearly 5,000 species of wingless parasitic insects.
Nicknamed sea cows, these slow-moving herbivorous mammals graze on more than 60 kinds of aquatic plants in the Caribbean, the Amazon basin, and West Africa — what are they?
Manatee: Genus of mammals. The main causes of death for manatees are human-related issues, such as habitat destruction and human objects.
Diagnosis, prognosis, prevention, treatment and palliation of injury and disease — drawing on biomedical science, genetics and technology — define this science and practice. What is it?

Medicine: Diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of illness. Medicine encompasses a variety of health care practices which evolved to maintain and restore health through the prevention and treatment of illness and infection.
Grouped by their small size and use of echolocation, this suborder of flying mammals turns out to be genetically distinct from its bigger, fruit-eating relatives — which creatures?

Thought to enjoy 'hybrid vigor' and a reduced risk of inbreeding-linked health problems, this catch-all term covers roughly 150 million dogs worldwide that don't belong to any officially recognized breed — what's it called?

When light from distant objects focuses in front of the retina rather than on it, far-away things blur while close ones stay sharp — and spending more time outdoors as a child seems to lower the risk. What's this refractive error?
Myopia: Inability to focus on distant objects.
This Danish physicist won the 1922 Nobel Prize for a model of the atom in which electrons leap between discrete, stable orbits around the nucleus — who is he?
Native to East Africa and known in some places as 'lady's fingers,' this mallow-family plant is prized for its edible green (sometimes red) seed pods — what is it?
Prized both as a delicacy and, in some species, for the pearls grown within its shell, which salt-water bivalve is this?
Oyster: Variety of families of Mollusca.
Whose name comes from Greek words for 'congealed' and 'curdled' — this plant-cell-wall polymer is extracted from citrus as a powder that makes jams and jellies set?
Pectin: Structural carbohydrate in the cell walls of land plants and some algae.
This branch of linguistics studies how spoken languages organize meaningful sound units — the kind of contrast that separates 'bat' from 'gnat' — what field is it?
Phonology: Study of sound organization in languages.
Its name comes from the Greek for 'making,' and it leans on devices like assonance, alliteration, and metre to evoke meanings beyond the literal — what literary art is this?

Detected by receptors in your muscles, tendons, and joints, this sense tells your brain where your body is in space, working alongside vision and balance to keep you upright and coordinated — what's it called?
Proprioception: Sense of self-movement, force, and body position.
Found in notable amounts in capers, red onions, and kale, this bitter-tasting plant flavonol is a popular ingredient in dietary supplements — what compound?
Quercetin: Chemical compound. It is found in many fruits, vegetables, leaves, seeds, and grains; capers, red onions, and kale are common foods containing appreciable amounts of it.

Found in fish, dairy, and meat, this fat-soluble vitamin A derivative is prescribed for xerophthalmia and used topically in anti-wrinkle skincare — but too much during pregnancy can harm the fetus. What is it?
Once used by German butchers to herd cattle and pull meat carts to market, this mastiff-type breed now works as a search-and-rescue and police dog — which breed?
Rottweiler: Large German dog breed. The Rottweiler (UK also, German: [ˈʁɔtvaɪ̯lɐ]) is a breed of domestic mastiff type dog, regarded as medium-to-large or large.

Discovered in 1879 via spectral analysis of Scandinavian minerals, this silvery-white rare-earth element with atomic number 21 wasn't isolated in metallic form until 1937, and today it's prized for strengthening aluminum alloys — which element?
Scandium: Chemical element with atomic number 21 (Sc)
Built with a ribless cartilage skeleton, skin-covering dermal denticles and five to seven gill slits per side, these fish first appeared back in the Devonian — what are they?
With the formula Na2SO4, this white, water-soluble compound is produced at six million tonnes a year and used as a filler in powdered laundry detergent — which compound?

Sodium sulfate: Chemical compound with formula Na2SO4. Sodium sulfate (also known as sodium sulphate or sulfate of soda) is the inorganic compound with formula Na2SO4 as well as several related hydrates.
This Polish-American DuPont chemist invented a super-strong polymer fiber and became the fourth woman ever inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame — who was she?
Stephanie Kwolek: American chemist who invented Kevlar (1923–2014)
Defined by a single skull opening behind each eye socket that anchors larger jaw muscles, this major branch of the amniote family tree includes all mammals and their extinct kin — which clade?
Synapsida: Clade of tetrapods. Synapsida is a diverse group of tetrapod vertebrates that includes all mammals and their extinct relatives.
Patented in 1953 and originally derived from Streptomyces bacteria, this antibiotic treats ailments from acne to cholera to plague by blocking bacterial protein production — which drug?
Tetracycline: Antibiotic. It is available in oral and topical formulations.
Home to more than 4,200 described species, this family of large crane flies can be identified by the length of their maxillary palps — what is it?
Tipulidae: Family of flies. There are more than 30 genera and 4,200 described species in Tipulidae, common and widespread throughout the world.
Element 74 boasts the highest melting point of any known element — a scorching 3,422 °C — and carries the symbol W from its German name. Which metal is it?
Tungsten: Chemical element with atomic number 74 (W)
The brightest star in the constellation Lyra, this star sits just 25 light-years away and served as Earth's northern pole star around 12,000 BCE — which star?
Vega: Brightest star in the constellation Lyra. It has the Bayer designation α Lyrae, which is Latinised to Alpha Lyrae and abbreviated Alpha Lyr or α Lyr.
With a distinctive pale eye and grey nape against black plumage, this small, gregarious member of the crow family was first formally described by Linnaeus — name the bird?
Western jackdaw: Species of bird in the crow family Corvidae.
Also called the pikeperch, this ray-finned game fish native to western Eurasian waters is the type species that gave its whole genus a name — which fish?
Zander: Species of fish. The zander (Sander lucioperca), sander or pikeperch, is a species of ray-finned fish from the family Percidae (which also includes perch, ruffe and darter).
What is the chemical symbol for sulfur?
The symbol for sulfur is S. Sulfur, also spelled as sulphur, is a chemical element; it has symbol S and atomic number 16.
What is the chemical symbol for rubidium?
The symbol for rubidium is Rb. Rubidium is a chemical element; it has symbol Rb and atomic number 37.

Richard Harris: Richard St John Francis Harris (1 October 1930 – 25 October 2002) was an Irish actor and singer.
In what year was Jet Li born?
Jet Li Lianjie (courtesy name Yangzhong; born 26 April 1963) is a martial artist, actor, and philanthropist.
In what year was Melanie Griffith born?
Melanie Griffith: Melanie Richards Griffith (born August 9, 1957) is an American actress.
In what year was Sofia Coppola born?
Sofia Coppola: Sofia Carmina Coppola ( KOH-pə-lə; born May 14, 1971) is an American filmmaker and former actress.
In what year was Sharon Tate born?
Sharon Tate: Sharon Marie Tate Polanski (January 24, 1943 – August 9, 1969) was an American actress and model.
In what year was Taika Waititi born?
Taika Waititi: Taika David Cohen (born 16 August 1975), known professionally as Taika Waititi ( TY-kə WY-tee-tee), is a New Zealand filmmaker, writer, actor, and comedian.
In what year was Nicholas Hoult born?
Nicholas Hoult: Nicholas Caradoc Hoult (born 7 December 1989) is an English actor.
In what year was Charles Bronson born?
Charles Bronson (born Charles Dennis Buchinsky; November 3, 1921 – August 30, 2003) was an American actor.
In what year was Sage Stallone born?
Sage Stallone: Sage Moonblood Stallone (May 5, 1976 – July 13, 2012) was an American actor.
In what year was Rashida Jones born?
Rashida Jones: Rashida Leah Jones ( rə-SHEE-də; born February 25, 1976) is an American actress and filmmaker.
